Stretched Thin: Majority of Americans Live Paycheck to Paycheck | The Report | US News
The Report
Stretched Thin
The continuing government shutdown highlights the fact that most Americans have little to no savings.
By Susan Milligan Senior Politics Writer Jan. 11, 2019, at 6:00 a.m.
(Brett Ziegler for USN&WR)
Paycheck to paycheck. It's a phrase that conjures up an image of people in unusual – and often temporary – circumstances. The single parent, trying to keep the rent paid and kids watched and fed with a job that offers flexibility, but not necessarily a good salary. The person without a college or even high school education, relegated to a minimum wage job. The family in which one parent has been laid off.
[
SEE:
Political Cartoons on the Government Shutdown ]
In fact, living paycheck to paycheck – meaning there's not a cash cushion to cover the bills if the income stops for awhile – is a common condition in America. In the 12 th richest nation in the world by per capita GDP, nearly 8 in 10 U.S. workers live paycheck to paycheck, according to a 2017 study by CareerBuilder, a human capital management firm. And the trend crosses over income groups: more than half of minimum wage workers said they needed to hold down two jobs to make ends meet, while one in 10 workers earning $100,000 or more yearly say they live paycheck to paycheck.
And if there's an emergency? A large number of Americans don't have an accessible stash of money to cover a substantial health care expense or car repair, studies show. The Federal Reserve Board in 2017 found that 44 percent of American households surveyed could not cover a $400 emergency expense. A separate BankRate study last year yielded similar results, finding that while 34 percent of those surveyed had experienced a major unexpected expense in the previous year, just 39 percent of those surveyed said they could tap $1,000 from savings to cover it.
"It's not just people who are low wage earners. People who are making what most of us would consider a decent salary are living this way," says Cameron Huddleston, life and money columnist for GoBankingRates, a personal finance website. Some people are living beyond their means, while others are struggling to keep up with exorbitant housing and health care costs, she says. "It stretches you thin, even if you do have a decent salary. It's hard to get by and build that reserve of emergency cash," Huddleston adds.
The private financial struggles have become more public in past few weeks, as some 800,000 federal workers are either furloughed or being required to show up for work without pay. Friday is the payday that the workers won't be getting a paycheck, and it's going to be a problem for many.
While such workers tend to be given back pay once Congress and the White House agree to a budget, "it's not for sure," says Edward Hill, a furloughed U.S. Census Bureau employee. "My credit card [payment] is due," along with other bills. "I need money now – not later," he says. In the past, furloughed workers have been given back pay, and the Senate last year approved legislation guaranteeing back pay. President Donald Trump also said this week that such workers would be given retroactive pay, but there is still nervousness within the federal workforce.
Experts agree that it's bad, and even dangerous, to be in a sustained situation of having little or no emergency savings (let alone adequate retirement savings). But just like the partially-shut down federal government, which relies on borrowing to stay afloat and risks another downgrading of its credit rating should the shutdown persist, Americans are unable, or unwilling, to live within their means, analysts say.
[
READ:
Senior Trump Officials to Get $10,000 Raises ]
Credit is much easier to get, and has become a convenience instead of an emergency tool, experts say. And while that can be helpful to, for example, a furloughed worker who uses the credit card to fill a gap between paychecks, it also likely encourages people to spend more.
"Many of us American spend on what brings us pleasure now, instead of thinking about the future," Huddleston says. So instead of saving up for the house down payment, or the nice vacation or fancy car, people take out loans and pay it off – seemingly interminably.
A study by CIT Bank last year, for example, found that 29 percent of Americans surveyed have taken an "extreme action" to finance a vacation, such as taking out a bank loan, going over the maximum on a credit card or cleaning out the savings account.
Economists also note the existence of what they call the "wealthy hand to mouth," people who have pricey assets, such as large homes or boats, but do not have much in cash flow. The economists also concluded that "consumption overreacts to predictable income growth" – meaning, people send more (too much) when they know money is coming in.
"People do tend to spend more when they are using the credit card, especially if it's credit card vs. cash, when you feel the pain more" Huddleston says. And when it comes to mortgages, people may buy more than they can afford, or buy before they are ready. "We've put this idea into people's head that when you're renting, you're throwing money away. You're not getting equity," she adds.
The debt burden has gotten so bad for Millennials (18-34-year olds) that one in five expects to die without ever paying it all off, according to a CreditCards.com report.
That doesn't mean the 78 percent of American workers CareerBuilder cites as living paycheck-to-paycheck are being irresponsible, financial analysts say. The minimum wage has not remotely kept up with inflation, making it exceedingly difficult for people to survive on it. Major living expenses, such as housing, health care and higher education, have also gone up well beyond inflation, making it more difficult for the average family – or even a better-than-average earner – to have the life their parents or grandparents did.
"There is a backdrop of rising inequality and wage stagnation for most workers since the 1970s," says Heidi Shierholz, former chief economist at the Department of Labor and now director of policy at the Economic Policy Institute. "We used to have an economy where every generation did better than the one which preceded it. You had a job that would let you put away a little for retirement and college and take a vacation, all while being able to live in a decent home in a safe neighborhood. All of that stuff is farther and farther out of reach for people."
The very high cost of housing in certain areas of the country also stretches the paychecks of what appear to many to be high-income earners. In Washington, D.C., for example, the median household income in 2017 was $97,148 annually, says Kali McFadden, senior research analysts at Lending Tree and Magnified Money, a personal finance site. That income still leaves those earners a few hundreds dollars short each month, given the cost of housing and transportation. (Magnified Money ranked the D.C. area as the tenth worst place to live on a six-figure income.)
[
PHOTOS:
The Government Shutdown ]
Further, the nation's capital is very highly educated – and that means more student debt, McFadden notes. And that's not a problem limited to D.C.
The debt-to-income ratio has gone down from its financial crisis-era peak, which is a positive sign for personal finance, says a Federal Reserve economist. But personal debt is moving away from mortgages and more towards student debt, the economist explains.
The Federal Reserve reported last year that outstanding student loan debt increased by $37 billion, to $1.44 trillion from the second to third quarters of 2018. For a furloughed federal workers with student debt, the threat could be even more long-lasting, McFadden says. Living paycheck to paycheck means that if you were to miss a paycheck, you wouldn’t have enough money to pay your bills.

1. Make a Zero-Based Budget
Making a zero-based budget is the foundation for everything you do with your finances. It will help you plan your money in order to achieve your goals.
A zero-based budget is simply planning for every dollar in your budget.
It helps you be more intentional with your money so you can reach your savings goals.
When you plan out your budget by planning every single dollar, you are able to see how much you really have left to save or pay towards debt.

You will also clearly see if you have a spending or an income problem.

Saving a small starter emergency fund is your buffer from disaster. If you have $1000 saved you are already ahead of 80% of Americans.

You will be able to pay some bills and have food and gas if for some reason your paycheck is delayed.
That is more than most people.

The less debt you have the less risk there is of losing your possession if something happens to your paycheck.
It lessens the amount of money you need in-between paychecks as well.
It really all around lessens your financial burden and allows you to do what you really want in life.

Total up all your debts from the smallest balance to the largest balance. Then get to work on the debt snowball.

By the time you get to your largest debt, you will have all your extra money plus all the minimum payments to put towards it every month.
